summary: This work demonstrates, to the best of our knowledge, the first passive-layer-free thin-film lithium tantalate (LT) actuator platform, supporting both out-of-plane flexural and in-plane torsional actuation from a single bilayer periodically poled piezoelectric film (P3F) X-cut LT stack. The polarity reversal across the bond interface flips the piezoelectric stress below the neutral axis, generating a bending moment without any passive elastic layer. Moreover, the two layers share identical elastic and thermal-expansion constants, making the stack thermally matched by construction. Suspended cantilever devices were fabricated on a single 2$\times$1.5 $μ$m X-cut LT stack and verified by laser Doppler vibrometry (LDV). The tapered flexural resonator exhibits a 5.5$\times$ tip velocity amplification and a measured peak tip velocity of 10.3 m/s at $Q=634$, and a 0.49 MHz torsional cantilever resonator with $Q=514$ is demonstrated on the same stack. These results position bilayer P3F LT as a thermally matched, passive-layer-free actuation platform for vacuum-operated and optically interrogated MEMS such as scanners, gyroscopes, and ultrasonic transducers.

title: DeNA-SGN: Deterministic Neighborhood Aggregation for Verified Spiking Graph Inference
summary: Graph learning on neuromorphic substrates requires an explicit spiking realization of neighborhood aggregation, supporting control and classification. We propose DeNA-SGN, which combines fixed OR and tie-inclusive Majority aggregation of binary node features with a learned signed-weight threshold classifier. A degree-dependent inhibitory construction implements Majority through shared control neurons, enabling a complete circuit compilation into SuperNeuroMAT. Across seven datasets and 41 mapped classifiers, native simulation matches the exported ANN on every evaluated class decision and output-spike pattern. On the new confirmatory Amazon Photo dataset, DeNA-SGN achieves 83.93+-0.93% current-readout accuracy and 71.61+-2.22% strict output-spike accuracy; Wiki-CS reaches 75.99+-0.54% over 20 public masks. In the matched Cora study, we achieve 74.90+-2.67% on current-readout and 68.57+-2.94% strict spike accuracy. Complete circuit and activity accounting supports analytical energy comparisons and identifies the cost of clocking inactive neurons in large deployments. Current argmax is decoded on the host, and energy is modeled rather than measured on hardware. These findings establish a reproducible route to useful graph classification with decision-matched spiking execution and explicit implementation costs.

title: On Ignorability Beyond Missing at Random: Completion-Invariant Missingness for Nonmonotone Missing Data
summary: The missing-at-random assumption underlies most analyses of incomplete data. Under nonmonotone missingness, it is especially stringent, imposing pattern-specific restrictions with different conditioning sets. A strictly weaker normalization condition is known to justify maximizing the observed-data likelihood. We show that every law satisfying this condition has a unique missing-at-random counterpart sharing its observed-data and complete-data distributions. Observed-data procedures developed under missing at random for identified functionals, including doubly robust estimators, therefore remain valid, with the same semiparametric efficiency bound. We then prove that the condition holds if and only if filling in the missing values from their conditional distribution under the true full model preserves the complete-data distribution, hence the name completion-invariant missingness. We use a characteristic kernel to compare the completed distribution with the fitted model and assess the joint compatibility of the specified full model and completion-invariant missingness. We derive the asymptotic null distribution with estimated parameters and establish bootstrap and multiplier calibration. Since a parametric full model alone need not identify completion-invariant missingness, we give identification conditions for Gaussian, Student $t$ and finite mixture families. Simulations assess sensitivity to departures from each assumption, and applications to clinical laboratory measurements and childhood growth illustrate the diagnostic.

title: Data-center growth impacts household electricity costs more through wholesale prices than through grid reinforcement
comment: 22 pages, 8 figures, 1 table. Lingdong Zhou and Wenjia Xia contributed equally to this work
summary: Rapid data-center expansion is raising concerns about electricity affordability, yet how the costs of serving these large new loads reach residential customers remains poorly understood. Here, we quantify the potential impact of 371 announced Texas data-center projects, totaling 38.9 GW by 2030, on residential electricity costs by linking power system expansion, wholesale electricity markets, transmission reinforcement, and retail cost allocation. We find that accommodating this demand increases modeled residential electricity costs in one representative case by 1.64 cents/kWh, with 68% arising from higher wholesale electricity prices and 32% from regulated transmission charges. Allowing new gas generation near data centers reduces the 2023 residential cost increase to 0.92 cents/kWh, whereas excluding data centers from the transmission cost-sharing base raises it to 1.87 cents/kWh. These findings reveal that the residential cost burden of data-center growth is driven primarily by wholesale electricity price increases, rather than direct transmission investment costs, and depends critically on generation siting, infrastructure planning, and cost allocation.

title: SlipStream: Enabling HBF for GPU Systems by Mitigating the Latency and SRAM Overheads
comment: To appear in 2027 IEEE International Symposium on High-Performance Computer Architecture (HPCA)
summary:
Large language model (LLM) inference demands ever more memory capacity for larger models and batch sizes. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) replaces the DRAM dies of HBM with NAND flash and provides up to 16x the capacity at comparable read bandwidth. However, HBF can incur a read latency of nearly 20$μ$s, 20x that of HBM, so on-demand HBF accesses slow inference by up to 12.8x. Conventional cache-line prefetchers require 20x more in-flight tracking state to cover this latency. Tensor-streaming designs, such as H3, follow virtual-address order as opposed to kernel-demand order, and therefore need hundreds of megabytes of buffering.
  We propose SlipStream, a software-hardware co-designed prefetcher that turns prefetching into a demand-paced producer-consumer pipeline. In software, SlipStream profiles the repeatable weight-page demand order of data-independent LLM kernels and inserts a staging warp that replays this order with non-blocking STAGE instructions. In hardware, the staging warp acts as the producer and the work warps as consumers. Our key insight is to retire each STAGE tracking entry only when demand first accesses the page, as opposed to when the page returns from HBF. Demand thus paces staging and bounds how far staging leads consumption. SlipStream tracks 4 KB pages instead of cache lines and allocates buffer slots only when pages return, which decouples the buffer size from outstanding traffic. Across seven dense models spanning 16-800 GB, SlipStream with a 40 MB staging buffer achieves 92.4% of the performance of an ideal HBF with HBM-like latency. H3 achieves only 43.1%, even with a 320 MB buffer. The buffer sizing of SlipStream is independent of HBF latency and workload. SlipStream with 16 MB buffer, 20x smaller than that of H3, performs within 4% of SlipStream-40MB. SlipStream also supports Mixture-of-Experts models and reaches 91.2% of ideal performance (40 MB buffer).

title: One-Sided Randomization in Two-Sided Platform Experiments: Which Side Should be Randomized?
summary:
Two-sided marketplace platforms often use randomized experiments to evaluate new features, raising the question of whether to randomize customers or listings. Randomizing the smaller (\emph{short}) side can reduce interference bias due to weaker competition, while randomizing the larger (\emph{long}) side provides a larger nominal sample, potentially reducing variance. On the surface, these competing considerations suggest a bias-variance trade-off in choosing which side to randomize. We investigate this trade-off in a two-sided marketplace with first-come, first-served (FCFS) booking and heterogeneous customer preferences, studying the bias and variance of difference-in-means estimators of the global average treatment effect.
  Our findings suggest that rather than a bias-variance tradeoff, in fact short-side randomization is generally preferable on {\em both} dimensions. We prove these results in an asymptotic regime where market imbalance increases. We establish conditions under which (1) short-side randomization eliminates first-order interference bias, while long-side randomization retains it; and (2) short-side randomization also achieves a variance rate of no larger asymptotic order than long-side randomization. The key insight is that although the long side contains more participants, the number of matches is constrained by the population on the short side, limiting the apparent variance advantage of randomizing a larger sample. Our conditions accommodate heterogeneous preferences and treatment effects and are satisfied by familiar logit models of customer choice. Together, these findings support randomizing on the short side, despite the larger sample size available on the long side.

title: Real-Time Low-Complexity Zak-OTFS with Superimposed Spread Pilots on GPUs
summary: Orthogonal time frequency space (OTFS) modulation offers robust performance under high-mobility scenarios. Spread pilots distribute pilot energy across the delay-Doppler grid and are superimposed with data symbols, enabling full-grid resource utilization. However, pilot-data separation challenges the design of the real-time receiver pipeline: cross-ambiguity in channel sensing incurs high computational complexity, and pilot-data interference cancellation requires repeated processing through turbo iterations. Leveraging the chirp structure of OTFS spread pilots, we reduce cross-ambiguity to a single 2D IFFT with element-wise chirp operations, achieving over 7000x speedup compared to partially vectorized direct evaluation on GPUs at a frame size of (M, N)=(2053, 31). Our real-time GPU baseband processing pipeline for OTFS with superimposed spread pilots supports (M, N)=(2053, 31) with one turbo iteration within a 1.03 ms latency budget. We further show that larger frames increase processing gain, allowing lower pilot power and near-converged bit error rate (BER) after one turbo iteration.

title: Mach2: Scientific Discovery Platform with Deterministic Execution Constraints
summary: Language-model agents can formulate workflows and invoke specialized tools, yet compliance with natural-language operating rules is not guaranteed by prompting alone. Mach2 addresses this limitation by coupling Eigen orchestration to deterministic, lint-like checks of tool requests, source changes, acceptance tests, and artifact contracts. Domain requirements are represented as executable predicates: mandatory failures prevent advancement of the checked operation, while diagnostic findings are retained for correction or review. User-specified test-driven development (TDD), CodeGrapher's abstract-syntax-tree analysis, and history-guided evolutionary search provide complementary verification and optimization mechanisms. Mach2 also generates task-specific agent packages for execution through independently selected endpoints. The originating harness validates returned artifacts against declared interfaces and evidence requirements without assuming continuous supervision of the remote run. Model-internal-knowledge (MIK) dependencies are recorded separately from source-grounded and test-supported findings. This paper formalizes the rule-gated execution model and the agent-package lifecycle, and proposes measurable criteria for evaluating rule compliance, engineering validity, and cross-endpoint task continuity.

title: Exact power spectra and effective dimensionality in critical block-GOE networks
summary: Criticality in neural networks is crucial for optimal information processing. Recent studies have shifted focus from static criticality to frequency-dependent behavior, particularly in oscillatory systems modeled by block-Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (block-GOE) matrices. However, analytical tools to predict spectral properties such as power spectrum and effective dimensionality remain scarce. In this work, we derive exact solutions for the network-averaged power spectrum $\operatorname{Tr}_{N}[\mathbf{S}(ω)]$, the network autocovariance $\operatorname{Tr}_{N}[\mathbf{C}(τ)]$, and the normalized effective dimensionality $D_N(ω)$ in block-GOE ensembles. These results provide a comprehensive framework for understanding how oscillatory networks operate near criticality, offering insights into the dynamic balance between stability and flexibility in large-scale neural systems.

title: Enabling Versatile Human Sensing through Wi-Fi Beamforming Feedback
summary: Wi-Fi sensing enables contactless human sensing, while most existing systems rely on Channel State Information, which is accessible only on a limited range of Wi-Fi chipsets. In contrast, Beamforming Feedback Information (BFI) is standardized in modern Wi-Fi and readily accessible on a wide range of commodity devices, offering new opportunities for human sensing. In this paper, we present BeamLens, a Wi-Fi sensing system that extracts fine-grained spatial information from BFI to enable versatile human sensing. Specifically, we jointly estimate the angle of departure and relative time of flight from BFI to extract fine-grained spatial information and leverage two AP-STA links to capture complementary azimuth and elevation views. We further design a sparse physical antenna array and construct a uniform virtual antenna array to enhance spatial resolution. Moreover, we fuse complementary views through self-supervised learning, combining temporally aware cross-view contrastive learning and temporal masked reconstruction to learn a versatile backbone for diverse human sensing tasks. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that BeamLens achieves 90.16\% accuracy in human activity recognition, a mean per-joint position error of 8.64\,cm in 3D human pose estimation, and 70.64\% intersection over union in human silhouette estimation, while exhibiting strong generalization to unseen environments and subjects.

title: Posterior contraction rates for banded approximations of Gaussian processes
summary:
Gaussian process regression models are widely used in modern statistics and machine learning due to their flexibility, interpretability, built-in uncertainty quantification, and strong theoretical foundations. However, training Gaussian processes (GPs) has a computational cost of $O(n^3)$, while the memory and prediction costs are also $O(n^2)$.
  For large datasets commonly encountered in practice, this becomes infeasible and necessitates the use of approximate posterior methods.
  In this work, we propose a class of approximations based on sparse covariance matrices, where the kernel matrix is sparsified according to the spatial proximity of the design points.
  We analyze the accuracy of the resulting approximate posterior distribution and show that the proposed approach preserves optimal statistical inference properties, provided that the dependencies among a sufficient number of neighboring points for each feature are retained.
  We derive explicit sufficient and necessary conditions on the number of neighbors required in a general setting and apply these results to standard kernels, including the squared exponential and Matérn kernels. Our theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments.

title: FGCARL: Fisher-Guided Continuously Adaptive Representation Learning for Medical Image Segmentation
summary: Deep learning (DL) has achieved remarkable success in medical image segmentation by learning data-driven representations from large-scale annotated datasets. However, medical images are often collected independently across clinical sites, resulting in substantial domain shifts due to differences in imaging modalities, acquisition protocols, and intensity distributions. Meanwhile, segmentation classes may vary across sites due to differences in annotation standards, leading to class shifts. These evolving domains and class definitions can substantially degrade segmentation performance on newly encountered data, while sequential adaptation may cause catastrophic forgetting of knowledge acquired from previously encountered domains and classes. Existing incremental learning methods for medical image segmentation primarily address either domain shifts or class shifts, with these two settings largely investigated independently. This separation leaves a critical gap in developing a unified approach that can simultaneously adapt to evolving domains and newly introduced classes while retaining previously acquired knowledge. To address this challenge, we propose Fisher-Guided Continuously Adaptive Representation Learning, a unified framework for domain- and class-incremental 3D volumetric medical image segmentation. FGCARL comprises two key components: Mutual Adaptive Instance Representation (MAIR), which adaptively aligns feature distributions across sequentially encountered domains through bidirectional normalization and denormalization, and Fisher-Guided Knowledge Retention (FGKR), which selectively preserves parameters important for previously learned domains and classes through Fisher-guided regularization. Experimental results demonstrate that FGCARL consistently outperformed state-of-the-art methods, effectively adapting to domain and class shifts while mitigating catastrophic forgetting.

title: RE-PRESENT: Evidence Triangulation across Alternative Candidate-Space Views for Efficient LLM Ensemble Inference
summary: Heterogeneous large language models (LLMs) exhibit complementary strengths, motivating routing and multi-model inference methods that seek to identify reliable predictions for each input. However, exploiting this complementarity remains challenging even when a correct prediction is available within the ensemble. We investigate this challenge across heterogeneous LLM ensembles and find that a simple single-round aggregation rule is highly competitive with learned routing methods, yet substantial oracle headroom remains. Further analysis shows that the evaluated single-round response signals provide limited discriminative power for identifying reliable predictions. In contrast, controlled re-presentations of the same question elicit complementary evidence about prediction reliability. Motivated by these findings, we introduce RE-PRESENT, a training-free framework that selectively re-presents disputed questions and directly aggregates candidate-level evidence across alternative views. Across seven multiple-choice benchmarks and two heterogeneous model ensembles, RE-PRESENT improves over strong single-round aggregation while offering a favorable accuracy--cost trade-off compared with self-consistency and multi-model debate.

title: Localizing Mean Shifts in High-Dimensional Vector Autoregressive Models
summary:
We study the localization of mean changes in high-dimensional vector autoregressions (VARs) when the autoregressive dynamics remain common across regimes. We develop a three-step procedure that first obtains preliminary change-point estimates from the raw series ignoring the dependence structure, then estimates a common sparse VAR using observations away from the estimated changes, and finally filters the series to refine the change point locations.
  For a single change point, we show that the preliminary localization rate depends directly on the strength of temporal dependence, whereas filtering removes this dependence penalty from the oracle rate. With an estimated filter, the refined rate additionally reflects the error in estimating the VAR dynamics and the relation between the change in the stationary mean and the corresponding change in the VAR intercept. We characterize these rates explicitly and establish conditions under which filtering improves localization. Because filtering near a change point uses lags from adjacent regimes, it also creates a short-lived distortion in the filtered mean; we characterize when this boundary effect is innocuous and develop a transition-corrected alternative.
  We extend the procedure to an unknown number of change points. Overlapping local windows are used to generate candidate locations, an information criterion removes redundant and spurious candidates and estimates the number of changes, and the retained locations are subsequently refined using the estimated VAR filter. We establish consistency for the estimated number of changes and simultaneous localization rates for their locations. Numerical experiments corroborate the localization gains and show robustness to moderate departures from common VAR dynamics. An application to a large panel of U.S. macroeconomic indicators identifies economically interpretable changes.

title: GridForge: A Tractable Network-Flow Method for Constructing Open, Continental-Scale Synthetic Power Grids
comment: 30 pages, 10 figures, 7 tables; supplementary material as an ancillary file. Submitted to the International Journal of Electrical Power & Energy Systems. Data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24096575; code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23826484
summary: The goal of this paper is to construct open, continental-scale synthetic transmission grids with an optimization method that stays tractable. Security restrictions keep models of the real grid out of open research and machine-learning datasets, and optimization-based construction is hard at scale: the number of candidate lines grows combinatorially, so electrically faithful methods prune the candidates in advance. This paper presents GridForge, which keeps every bus pair within physical length limits as a candidate, selects lines with Garver's length-weighted network-flow linear program instead of binary decisions, and resizes them with a sequential direct-current (DC) power flow. Two stages of 13 regional networks are evaluated. Their node-degree distributions are nearly as strongly log-linear as those of the real Eastern and Western Interconnections ($R^2$ of 0.92 to 0.98 against 0.971 and 0.981), although the areas under the fitted lines differ from the real ones by 39.9% on average. On the upper Midwest and Tennessee Valley footprints, resizing lowers the DC power-flow loss from 5.89% to 4.14% and from 14.55% to 7.05%, and the DC optimal power-flow loss from 4.03% to 2.02% and from 5.54% to 2.47%. Without relaxing any line limit, the DC optimal power flow is feasible in 78.81% and 0.82% of the scenarios. Most lines are built at 69 kV. The models span 250 to 78,484 buses, were built on single machines, and are freely redistributable.

title: Robust Task-Aware State Estimation from Pre-trained Perception
comment: The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 2026
summary: Agents that perform state estimation using pretrained perception models, e.g., Vision-Language Models (VLMs), face the fundamental challenge that predictions are uncertain. Still, most approaches determinize these predictions into a single best-guess state and make decisions as if it were ground truth. This is brittle because when the guess is wrong, the agent's decisions may be unsafe or infeasible. At the other extreme, maintaining a full probability distribution over symbolic states is often intractable. We propose a middle path, drawing on the underlying probabilities the perception model already produces (e.g., a VLM's output-layer token distributions) to construct a $θ$-confidence Minimal Belief Set (MBS$_θ$), a minimal subset of states whose cumulative probability meets a user-specified belief-mass threshold. The minimality of an MBS$_θ$ ensures that the agent considers only the most likely states, enhancing robustness in downstream decision-making while maintaining computational tractability. Using a novel three-layered belief system, we efficiently approximate individual state probabilities from per-feature predictions and task-level constraints. On this belief construction, we base our MBS$_θ$ construction, while maintaining only a lean factored representation of the belief. Our algorithm, Probability-Ranked Valid State Search (PRaVaSS), takes advantage of the unique structure of this belief system to construct an MBS$_θ$ with correctness guarantees and polynomial complexity in the unconstrained case. Using a VLM as the backbone of our state estimator, we validate our method's theoretical properties, scalability with problem size, and improvement of downstream decision-making when used in a task-planning pipeline.

title: Inverse Confounding Analysis: Part 2. Applications to Real- World Observational Data
summary: Unmeasured confounding factors in observational data may lead to biased estimates of the effect of an exposure on an outcome. Consequently, a central problem in causal inference based on observational data is sensitivity analysis with respect to unmeasured confounding. Existing sensitivity-analysis methods generally focus on worst-case bounds. We propose an exact method for quantifying the significance of confounding, defined here in terms of the complete range of analytical values of the stratification-based Risk Ratio over the set of all joint distributions compatible with the observed characteristics. We refer to the proposed method as Inverse Confounding Analysis (ICA) - it is described in [1]. This paper presents examples of applying ICA to several real-world statistical datasets and examines an important issue that has attracted criticism of the method: the practical feasibility of obtaining the input data required for its application. The results are compared with those of two other methods for confounding analysis, the E-value and the method proposed by Pena.

title: DER Aggregators in Wholesale Electricity Markets: A Hybrid Mean-Field Framework with Endogenous Price Feedback
summary: The rapid growth of distributed energy resources (DERs), including rooftop solar and energy storage, is transforming the grid edge, where customer-side assets increasingly interact with the broader power grid. DER aggregators, entities that coordinate the actions of many small-scale DERs, play a key role in this transformation. This paper presents a hybrid Mean-Field Control (MFC) and Mean-Field Game (MFG) framework for integrating DER aggregators into wholesale electricity markets. Unlike traditional approaches that treat market prices as exogenous, our model captures the feedback between aggregators' collective actions and electricity prices. The MFC component optimizes DER operations within each aggregator, while the MFG models strategic interactions among multiple aggregators. To account for various uncertainties, we incorporate reinforcement learning, which allows aggregators to learn optimal bidding strategies in dynamic market conditions. We prove the existence and uniqueness of a mean-field equilibrium and validate the framework through a case study of the Oahu Island power system. Results show that our approach reduces price volatility and improves market efficiency, offering a scalable and decentralized solution for DER integration in wholesale markets.

title: Bayesian inference with a polymer probabilistic computer
comment: 21 pages, 4 figures, 1 table, plus Supplementary Information (3 notes, 1 figure)
summary: Bayesian inference weighs competing explanations of noisy data by sampling from a posterior distribution, a task that deterministic hardware performs only by simulating randomness. Probabilistic bits (p-bits) supply this randomness physically, but the few hardware networks of p-bits built so far use inorganic devices, address optimization or learning, and are judged without reference to the spread expected from finite sampling. Here we report a probabilistic computer built from solution-processed conjugated-polymer memristors. Four polymer p-bits, tracked online for drift and coupled in a closed Gibbs-sampling loop, sample competing, degenerate and cooperative posteriors over sixteen states with statistics that fall within the range of ideal p-bits, both in their distribution and in their autocorrelation, without any parameter fitted to the target. This agreement extends to new simulated sensor readings whose outcome was predicted before each run, including readings that point away from the true answer. Reprogrammed in software, the same circuit and controller reproduces the invertible AND gate of earlier p-bit networks, with its temperature fixed in advance rather than fitted. Polymer p-bits thus open a route to printed, large-area probabilistic computers that infer alongside their sensors.

title: When and How SignSGD Outperforms SGD: A Functional Scaling Law Perspective
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 as a spotlight paper
summary: We study how the sign operator interacts with gradient noise to shape the learning dynamics and scaling behavior of sign-based optimizers. In power-law kernel regression with diagonal features, we establish a functional scaling law (FSL) for SignSGD under general learning rate schedules. The FSL describes the learning dynamics through two processes: signal learning and noise forgetting. The key mechanism is noise-induced preconditioning: gradient noise smooths the sign operator, inducing an effective preconditioned SGD. Noise-curvature alignment enables this preconditioning to transform the effective Hessian from $\mathbf{H}$ to $\mathbf{H}^{1/2}$. The resulting dynamics exhibit faster signal learning but slower noise forgetting than SGD. This tradeoff yields a regime-dependent comparison with SGD: (i) SignSGD achieves improved data efficiency in the hard-task regime; (ii) both optimizers achieve the same data efficiency in the easy-task regime, but SignSGD maintains this efficiency at larger batch sizes, requiring fewer optimization steps for a fixed data budget. Power-law kernel regression experiments support the proposed mechanism and predicted scaling behavior. LLM pre-training experiments further suggest that the SignSGD FSL better captures the batch-size dependence of loss dynamics for sign-based optimizers than the original SGD FSL.

title: Cost of Decibel-Domain Averaging of Line-of-Sight States in Aerial Coverage Analysis
summary: Uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) coverage studies routinely average the line-of-sight (LoS) and non-line-of-sight (NLoS) path loss in the decibel domain, weighted by their probabilities. Since the conditional path-loss distribution is bimodal, the resulting mean path loss describes no physical link. We give the error of this mean path loss, relative to the path loss that corresponds to the mean received power, in closed form. We quantify it by ray tracing an ITU-R P.1410 city, supplying the averaged model with the exact LoS probability so that no parameter error contributes. Our numerical results show that the averaged path loss is 6.6 dB higher than the path loss of the mean received power and lies within 2 dB of only 6.2% of the links. It moves the coverage-optimal altitude from 1764 m to 778 m and understates the outage probability by up to 0.198.

title: A Multi-Prover Interactive Protocol for Certification of Resolution Refutations
comment: 33 pages, 7 figures, extended version to CSL 2027 version
summary: A resolution refutation of a SAT-formula $\varphi$ is an independently checkable certificate proving that $\varphi$ is unsatisfiable. However, the refutations of $\varphi$ can be exponentially larger than $\varphi$. So, a verifier needs worst-case exponential time in the size of $\varphi$ to check their correctness. We present ResCertify, an interactive probabilistic protocol in which the verifier interacts with multiple independent, untrusted provers (MIP) to check the refutation with very low probability of error. The verifier runs in linear time in the size of $\varphi$. The provers require time $\mathcal{O}(n \cdot |Φ|)$, where $Φ$ is the resolution refutation and $n$ is the number of variables of $\varphi$. If they can be trusted to act as a multilinear oracle on certain queries, a single prover suffices, and the runtime can be improved to $\mathcal{O}(|Φ|)$. Finally, while the focus of our work is theoretical, we also report on a proof-of-concept implementation of ResCertify.

title: Estimation and Inference for Multiplicative Error Models via Analytical Derivatives
summary: Maximum Likelihood Estimates (MLEs) of the parameters of a Multiplicative Error Model are typically computed through a standard gradient method, an iterative procedure usually based on numerical approximations to derivatives of the log-likelihood function, owing to the complexity of the analytical derivatives, which involve recursive terms. Building on previous work developed mainly in the GARCH framework, we derive analytical expressions for the score vector and the Hessian matrix of the Multiplicative Error Model log-likelihood by adopting the Gamma distribution for estimation purposes. Then, we illustrate how the iterative algorithm based on the analytical derivatives should be computationally implemented. After maximizing the log-likelihood, we also provide explicit formulas for several estimators of the asymptotic covariance matrix of the MLE. Additionally, we provide analytic formulas for robust covariance estimators that remain valid under distributional misspecification, which are also referred to as the asymptotic variance of the Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimator. We also propose a covariance estimator that is consistent under general forms of heteroskedasticity of the error term, while the usually adopted estimators rely on a specific variance assumption. The finite-sample performance of the covariance estimators is assessed through a Monte Carlo investigation. An application on real data completes the analysis.

title: A Theoretical Framework for Frequency-Shift Filtering-Based Interference Mitigation for OFDM Systems
summary: Orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) is widely adopted in modern wireless systems due to its high spectral efficiency and robustness to multipath propagation. However, its performance can be severely degraded by narrowband and wideband interference, particularly in spectrally congested environments where interference overlaps significantly in time and frequency with the desired signal. In this paper, we investigate interference mitigation for OFDM signals using the FREquency-SHift (FRESH) filter, which exploits cyclostationarity inherent to the waveform or induced by the modulation design. By leveraging correlations between frequency-shifted versions of the received signal, the FRESH filter provides optimal linear filtering for the cyclostationary processes. We first analyze the second-order statistics of OFDM signals with known structure and characterize their cyclostationary properties. Based on this analysis, we derive a compact closed-form matrix expression for the optimal FRESH filter coefficients under the minimum mean-square error (MMSE) criterion. The proposed framework enables offline computation of the filter coefficients when the signal structure is known and interference parameters are estimated, thereby reducing real-time implementation complexity. Numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in suppressing interference and improving detection performance compared to conventional approaches.

title: Source Assignment: Hardness, Approximation, and Parameterized Algorithms
summary:
In Source Assignment, each pointer represents a substring of a common reference string and may have several possible source occurrences. The goal is to choose one source for each pointer while minimizing the number of distinct reference boundaries used by the selected sources. The problem was introduced by Qiu and Kingsford (Bioinformatics 2021) in the context of compact genome-graph construction. We distinguish \emph{Explicit Source Assignment}, where admissible source sets are given explicitly, from \emph{Complete Source Assignment}, where all occurrences of each pointer string are available.
  We show that Explicit Source Assignment has an exact value-preserving formulation as cardinality Set Cover with Pairs. For every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, it cannot be approximated within $(1-\varepsilon)\ln p$ unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, even over a binary alphabet when all pointers have length one, while known algorithms for Minimum-Weight Multicolored Subgraph give an $O(\sqrt{q\log p})$-approximation for arbitrary pointer lengths. Our main hardness result proves that Complete Source Assignment is APX-hard even over a binary alphabet, with equal pointer lengths and at most two sources per pointer. For edge-disjoint equal-length instances, we give a $3/2$-approximation and a $1.12585$-approximation when each pointer has at most two sources. We also introduce the rainbow-path length $λ$: the problem is polynomial-time solvable for $λ\le2$, and for $λ\le3$ we obtain a $(9/8+\varepsilon)$-approximation.
  We further give a polynomial-time test for deciding whether abstract source sets can be realized exactly as complete occurrence sets over an unrestricted alphabet. Finally, we give exact fixed-parameter algorithms for several structural parameters, and show that Complete Source Assignment is fixed-parameter tractable in the alphabet size and maximum pointer length.

title: Flexible nonlinear spatial autoregressive models under spatial confounding: a gradient boosting approach with closed-form estimation
summary: This paper develops a boosting-based framework for estimating nonlinear spatial autoregressive models (SAR and SEM). Functional gradient descent boosting with spline base learners provides automatic selection of covariates and functional forms, while the spatial parameter is estimated by an extension of the closed-form, determinant-free estimator (CFE) of Smirnov (2020): we show that it remains consistent, with the same asymptotic variance formula, for any additive estimator admitting a smoothing-matrix representation, and we prove that the underlying quasi-score is Neyman-orthogonal to the nonlinear nuisance, which makes the flexible, regularized first stage safe. This flexibility, however, exposes the estimator to a spatial confounding problem that must be solved for the framework to deliver structural estimates. The geoadditive smooth of the coordinates, s(u, v), a default ingredient of flexible spatial specifications, competes with the autoregressive term for the same low-frequency spatial variation, and purely predictive tuning resolves the competition in favour of the surface, biasing the spatial parameter -the geoadditive trap. We therefore equip the estimator with targeted safeguards: a spectral identification diagnostic, a spectral penalty on the surface, spatial cross-fitting, stopping iterations selected by spatial cross-validation, and heteroskedasticity-and spatial-correlation-robust sandwich variances. Monte Carlo experiments, including a factorial design that generates the trap, show that the safeguarded estimators restore test size and confidence-interval coverage while matching maximum likelihood accuracy at a fraction of its computational cost. An empirical application to the Lucas County, Ohio, housing market illustrates the workflow.

title: Physics-Aware Transformer-Based Beamforming Optimization for Near-Field E-MIMO ISAC Systems
summary: This paper proposes a physics-aware Transformer-based beamforming optimization (PATBO) framework for near-field extreme massive multiple-input multiple-output integrated sensing and communication (E-MIMO-ISAC) systems. PATBO combines regularized zero-forcing (RZF) communication directions and spherical-wave near-field sensing directions with learned stream-power allocation. A token-preserving Transformer maintains the correspondence between individual users/targets and their allocated powers, while a Cramér--Rao bound (CRB)-sensitivity-aware objective emphasizes power-allocation errors with greater localization impact. Physical feasibility is explicitly verified after inference, with infeasible predictions handled through physics-constrained power repair and optimizer fallback. For a $32\times32$ E-MIMO array with $1024$ antennas, the proposed structured representation reduces the learned output from $12{,}288$ real-valued coefficients of an unstructured complex beamformer to six stream-power variables. Direct PATBO achieves $100.98\%$ reference-rate retention and $19.54\%$ joint feasibility, which increases to $87.79\%$ after repair. The complete hybrid framework achieves $99.89\%$ reference-rate retention and $100\%$ constraint satisfaction on the retained test set, while requiring optimizer fallback for only $12.21\%$ of the scenarios. Direct PATBO inference requires $1.11$~ms per sample, corresponding to approximately $858\times$ and $779\times$ lower runtime than the evaluated cold-start and PATBO-warm-start sequential quadratic programming (SQP) implementations, respectively.

title: When Is Proof-Step Verification Worth Its Cost? Operating Requirements of Certify-or-Decline Verification for Open-Weight Mathematical Reasoning
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure, 13 tables. Accepted at the 6th Workshop on Mathematical Reasoning and AI (MATH-AI) at NeurIPS 2026. Code: https://github.com/yashica-patodia/certify-or-decline
summary: Proof-step verification rewrites a solver's answer into typed steps and uses LLM judges to certify or decline. We evaluate this pipeline on open-weight models across GPQA, AIME-2025, and a MATH-500 subset. Certification raises answer-key-match precision by 31 percentage points on the strong GPQA configuration and 46 on AIME, while answering only 35% and 21% of attempts. On near-ceiling MATH-500, gains are at most 5 points at a loss of 13-27 points of coverage. An output-token-matched self-consistency selector obtains 82.9% precision at 35% coverage, compared with the verifier's pooled 87.6% (paired difference: +4.8 points, 95% interval [-8.2, 18.5]). A diagnostic sample reveals a distinct failure mode: 52 of 88 completed problems end in invalid proof construction without ever reaching a judge. Finally, external-LLM acceptance of rendered certified chains is 61.0-67.6%, compared with 87.6% answer-key match. These audits lack human or formal-kernel ground truth. Open-weight auditor pairs show near-zero chance-corrected agreement, which measures consistency rather than accuracy against proof truth. These results motivate separate reporting of execution failures, selected-answer precision, and independently assessed proof validity. We provide per-configuration results and evaluation details in the supplement.

title: AIDA: Analysis of Interval Data in R
summary: AIDA is an R package that provides tools for the analysis of interval-valued data, including construction, visualization, robust estimation, and explainable outlier detection. The package is built around the intData class and is designed to support methodological research and applied workflows involving interval-valued data. AIDA implements methods for symbolic covariance estimation based on the Mallows distance, robust estimation via the Interval Minimum Covariance Determinant estimator, and explainable outlier detection using Shapley values. The package also includes visualization tools to support interpretation of the results and several interval-valued datasets.

title: Structured Speaker Conditioning for Diarization-Guided Target-Speaker ASR
summary: We propose structured speaker conditioning (SSC) for diarization-guided target-speaker recognition. SSC combines local activity structure with session-level acoustic identity to construct identity-consistent target conditions that control the acoustic encoder. Target-centric relational encoding (TCRE) retains per-speaker activity histories and factorized second- and third-order relations, capturing overlap and turn changes with aggregation cost linear in the number of tracks. Reference-based speaker conditioning (RSC) supplies session-derived identities that disambiguate local activity patterns within TCRE. Conditional low-rank modulation (CLRM) converts the joint condition into channel-wise affine modulation and a low-rank cross-channel residual with a condition-dependent core. On Qwen3-ASR-0.6B with oracle diarization, SSC uses 1.46M conditioning parameters and achieves a 6.23% mean relative reduction in concatenated minimum-permutation error rate (cpER) over four-state diagonal conditioning across four meeting test sets. SSC also transfers across audio foundation models. With predicted diarization and target-error group sequence policy optimization, the FireRedAudio text system achieves mean relative error reductions of 17.9% and 17.3% over DiCoW and MOSS-TD on the same four sets, and also outperforms both on three unseen domains. Scenario analyses identify gains under challenging overlap conditions, while fixed-checkpoint interventions support the contributions of session identity and the condition-dependent core. A timestamp variant jointly produces sentence boundaries and text. With predicted diarization, macro-average cpER across the four sets is 15.60% for text and 15.96% with timestamps.

title: Model Checking Probabilistic Multiparty Session Types
comment: 108 pages, full version of "Model Checking Probabilistic Multiparty Session Types" appearing at POPL 2027
summary: Distributed systems increasingly rely on randomisation; yet, verification techniques for such systems remain separate from the programming abstractions used to build them. This paper proposes the first probabilistic extension of general multiparty session types - typing sessions bottom-up, with no global specification - deriving quantitative properties of a multiparty session from its session types alone. Our types combine probabilistic choice with nondeterministic choice that abstracts data-dependent control, and allow separated choices, where each branch of a selection or branching may involve a different participant - a combination beyond previous probabilistic multiparty session type systems. To achieve this, we develop a novel probabilistic subtyping relation and merge operator, using which we prove type soundness and session fidelity. The semantics of typing contexts separates nondeterministic resolution, probabilistic choice, and synchronisation, so that every typing context induces a finite Markov decision process. On it, we derive sound lower bounds, holding under every fair adversarial scheduler, on the probability that a session is deadlock-free and live - the first behavioural property guarantees, partial or otherwise, for a probabilistic session calculus. To connect session types with probabilistic model checking, we introduce the first translation from session types into the PRISM modelling language, and prove it sound and complete with respect to our operational semantics. We implement the framework in the toolchain Prose, which translates probabilistic multiparty session typing contexts into PRISM and checks safety, deadlock-freedom, and liveness.

title: Parameter estimation in models with explosive drift and Gaussian noise
summary: We study drift parameter estimation for a positive stochastic process with singular mean-reverting drift driven by Gaussian noise. For Riemann-Liouville fractional Brownian noise with Hurst parameter $H>1/2$, an observable fractional transformation reduces the model to a semimartingale with drift linear in the unknown parameters. Using the quasi-likelihood approach, we derive explicit estimators of both drift coefficients. For a broader class of Gaussian driving processes, we construct a strongly consistent estimator of the ratio $a/b$, which has a natural mean-reversion interpretation, and verify the required assumptions for several Gaussian models. The theoretical results are complemented by a simulation study investigating the effects of the observation horizon and the discretization step on the finite-sample accuracy of the proposed estimators.

title: On Energy-Based Modelling for Fluidic Excitable Neurons
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, submitted to European Control Conference 2027
summary: Motivated by the potential of pneumatic excitable devices in soft robotics, this paper develops an energy-based, domain-agnostic equivalent of the Hodgkin-Huxley modelling framework using bond graph theory. The proposed model is used to guide the design of a pneumatic excitable neuron. The potential of this approach is illustrated through the design of a pneumatic half-center oscillator, an essential building block for rhythmic neuromorphic behaviours.

title: Selecting and verifying load-bearing periodic cells for elastic-wave band gaps with numerical acceptance checks
summary: A lattice mount must be stiff enough to support equipment and block vibration over a specified frequency range. Fast simulations help rank designs, but their errors can lead to a wrong acceptance decision. We present AMM (AgenticMetamaterials), an open-source Python tool that searches repeating cubic cells for targets on stiffness, the fraction of the cell that is solid, and band gaps. A complete band gap is an interval with no elastic-wave propagation in any direction. A separate checker allows for changes as the simulation grid gets finer. For gaps, it also tests for modes at sampled wave directions and wavelengths, so it can miss modes between samples. In 1,500 near-threshold tests of stiffness and solid fraction, the checker accepted 454 of 750 claims supported by the reference and none of the 750 false claims. Using the finest grid estimate alone accepted 42 false claims. In an independent finite-element comparison on ten new cells built from cubes joined by bars, the checker accepted one of two true gap claims and left all 17 false claims undecided. The reference could not classify the remaining claim. The protocol required every reported edge to err on the side of a narrower gap. The checker failed this test when it placed one upper edge too high, even though it left that thin-bar cell's claim undecided. Separating search from acceptance shows which targets the evidence supports and where a calculation needs further refinement.

title: Automatic Threshold Selection Leaves Finite-Degree Bias in Network Power-Law Fits
summary: Minimum-distance fitting selects a degree threshold and a power-law exponent from the same network. We study the procedure that fits a continuous Pareto law with the Hill estimator and minimizes the Kolmogorov--Smirnov distance over retained ranks. For homogeneous linear preferential attachment and Norros--Reittu graphs with Pareto weights, we derive the joint limiting law of the selected rank, retained fraction of the threshold tie, and exponent error. The selector retains of order $n^{2/(α+2)}$ of $n$ vertices, where $α$ is the survival exponent. At this rank, integer spacing and finite-degree departures from a Pareto tail have the same order as sampling fluctuations. The exponent estimate is consistent and retains a shift on the scale used for confidence intervals. For integer degree laws whose tail sums have a first-order inverse-degree expansion, adding the retained tie fraction divided by the threshold to the Hill statistic removes the leading contribution of the tie. Under homogeneous preferential attachment with a fixed known number of edges per new vertex, removing the remaining model-specific term and calibrating for selection gives confidence intervals with asymptotically exact coverage. Observed networks show sensitivity of the fitted exponent and the classification of degree variance to threshold ties. Simulations assess interval coverage and show improved pooled connectivity predictions after correction under both specified graph laws. Changes to the Norros--Reittu weight distribution can reverse the prediction gain.

title: Flexible Intelligent Metasurfaces for Enhancing Secure MISO Communications
summary: This letter investigates flexible intelligent metasurface (FIM)-aided secure multiple-input single-output (MISO) communications in the presence of a multi-antenna eavesdropper. By exploiting the morphing capability of the FIM, the transmit array geometry can be dynamically reconfigured to reshape the legitimate and eavesdropping channels. We formulate a secrecy rate maximization (SRM) problem by jointly optimizing the transmit covariance matrix and the FIM surface shape. For a given FIM surface shape, the optimal transmit covariance matrix is shown to be rank one and is obtained in closed form from the dominant generalized eigenvector. For a fixed transmit covariance matrix, a projected gradient ascent (PGA) method is developed to optimize the FIM shape. Based on these two subproblems, a block coordinate ascent (BCA) algorithm is proposed. Moreover, for the special line-of-sight (LoS) scenario, we derive a globally optimal closed-form joint transmit covariance matrix and FIM surface shape design under a sufficient morphing-range condition. Numerical results demonstrate that FIM effectively improves the secrecy rate over a conventional rigid antenna array (RAA). Moreover, FIM achieves a transmit-power saving of about 2.5 dB compared with the RAA benchmark at the same secrecy rate.

title: Who (or what) are they prompting? How CS students conceptualize and use LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by students in computing courses. Yet computing education research has not fully examined how teaching and inclusion of LLMs shape students' conceptualization and understanding of LLMs, and how these factors relate to their subsequent use. Although prior work has examined prompting strategies and AI literacy, the relationships among students' conceptualizations of LLMs, their understanding of LLM mechanisms, and their prompting behavior remain underexplored. We studied these relationships in a post CS1 course that introduces students to the various CS subfields. We adapted the course to teach and allow the usage of LLMs. We administered an end-of-course survey, using open-ended items to elicit students' representations of LLMs and their explanations of how LLMs work, alongside closed-response measures of prompting style and prompt count (N=283 students consented and provided codable responses). Using qualitative coding, we categorized students' understanding of how LLMs work into four ordinal knowledge levels based on the Structure of Observed Learning Outcomes (SOLO) taxonomy and coded their metaphoric conceptualizations along two dimensions: persona type and relational role. Our results show that students most often conceptualized LLMs as human assistants, and context-rich prompting was the preferred style. The study contributes a two-dimensional characterization of students' LLM metaphoric representation and exploratory analyses also identified associations among these constructs showing how understanding these systems relates to their usage.

title: A Class of Bayesian Conjugate Distributions on $SE_n(3)$ for Motion Estimation
summary: This paper proposes a novel class of Bayesian Conjugate Distributions (BCDs) on extended special Euclidean groups SE_n(3) for global motion uncertainty representation and estimation. BCDs are constructed by restricting matrix Gaussian distributions on ambient Euclidean space to SE_n(3), avoiding singularity of local coordinates. The unique feature of BCDs is their conjugacy to a broad class of sampling distributions arising in motion estimation, enabling exact closed-form Bayesian inference. Optimal estimation with respect to BCDs is further investigated for implementing motion estimation. Two means are extracted as random state estimates, which maximize probability and minimize mean squared error, respectively. Moreover, within the BCD class, moment matching is shown to minimize the Kullback-Leibler divergence, and maximum likelihood estimation is also derived, which provide analytical methods to approximate underlying distributions with the optimality guarantee. As an application, a Bayesian estimator for pose and velocity estimation of an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) is developed within an assumed density filtering architecture. The propagation and estimate extraction leverage the optimal estimation related to BCDs, and the landmark measurements are exactly fused with the BCD prior in closed form due to the conjugacy. Numerical simulations of a UAV flight indicate the advantages of BCD-based estimators over two classic Kalman filters on Lie groups with various initial uncertainties and measurement noise.

title: Synergizing Data-Driven Learning and Physical Rendering for Radio Map Prediction
summary: Accurate urban radio map prediction is challenging due to complex building geometries and sophisticated electromagnetic interactions. To address this, we propose a data- and physics-driven framework that decouples wave propagation from environmental feature extraction. The core idea is to predict a sparse set of low-dimensional Secondary Reradiation Points (SRPs), which, together with a closed-form renderer deduced from electromagnetic theory, yields the final radio map. By learning these SRPs end-to-end rather than directly regressing the high-dimensional map, the neural network focuses on a compact physical parameterization, significantly improving accuracy and generalization. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our framework outperforms all seven baselines and consistently yields the lowest errors across all building-coverage quintiles, underscoring its robustness in dense, heavily obstructed urban environments.

title: Distributionally Robust BEST-RQ For Speech Representation Learning
summary: BEST-RQ, based on random projection and quantization, has been a well-established self-supervised learning approach to learn speech representations from large-scale unlabeled audio due to its high performance and efficiency. However, in BEST-RQ representations learned by random quantization can be sensitive to the choice of quantization targets. To address this issue, we propose a distributionally robust extension of BEST-RQ that seeks representations robust across multiple quantization configurations. Specifically, we define groups by codebooks and formulate the training as a group Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) problem. Rather than optimizing solely for the average loss across groups, our approach adaptively reweights groups to emphasize those performing poorly. Additionally, we regularize DRO with a Kullback-Leibler divergence to prevent excessive distribution deviation. We evaluate our approach on the Multilingual LibriSpeech dataset and show that the distributionally robust BEST-RQ achieves superior performance over the conventional uniform average across multiple codebooks.

title: Functional Regression with Interacting Latent Mean and Variance Processes
summary: In many applications, variability itself carries important predictive information beyond the mean, and its association with an outcome may further depend on the underlying mean trajectory. However, existing functional regression approaches primarily rely on mean-based representations of functional predictors, while variability is often ignored or reduced to scalar summaries. We propose a functional regression framework that incorporates latent mean and variance processes as predictors, together with their mean-variance interaction, allowing the predictive contribution of variability to depend on the underlying mean trajectory. We establish consistency and convergence rates for the estimated coefficient functions and interaction surface, accounting for reconstruction errors, increasing observation frequency, and diverging truncation dimensions without requiring independence between the latent processes. Applications to real data demonstrate substantial gains in predictive accuracy from incorporating the variance process, with the proposed approach outperforming competing functional regression methods in the Tecator application and revealing localized mean-variance interaction patterns.

title: A Joint LLM and Optimization Agent Solution for Drone Scheduling in Victim Search Missions
summary: Victim search in wilderness areas is time-critical. Drones enable rapid area search, but scheduling them is challenging because victims may continue moving, detection results are uncertain, and effective decisions must combine structured mission information with unstructured contextual clues and domain knowledge. To address this, we propose an agent-aided drone scheduling system. The system employs an agent at the ground control station (GCS) to coordinate multiple drones over successive search cycles. In each cycle, the agent applies a scheduling policy that combines a large language model (LLM) for reasoning about where to search with an optimizer for determining how to dispatch the drones under energy constraints. Simulation results show that the proposed system consistently completes the victim-search mission, whereas none of the six non-LLM baselines does so and direct LLM scheduling is considerably less reliable. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/1643204431/llm-uav-victim-search.

title: GenPFN: An In-Context Tabular Foundation Model Approach for Augmenting Small Datasets in Engineering
summary:
Costly simulations and experiments limit the data available for engineering design. This paper proposes GenPFN, a training-free candidate generator guided by a pretrained tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN) classifier with fixed weights. The context contains evaluated designs labeled desired (Class 1) or undesired (Class 0). GenPFN interpolates between desired designs and refines candidates using gated classifier gradients and Gaussian noise. Each candidate is evaluated using the problem's constraints and objective functions. Evaluated desired designs and their objective values augment the context for regression training.
  Evaluation spans fourteen selected problems, including a two-parameter benchmark and a 44-parameter hull problem. In paired comparisons, GenPFN with TabPFN v1 achieves higher class satisfaction and lower realism distance than the tested adversarial, variational-autoencoder and diffusion generators. The variational-autoencoder generator provides greater coverage and diversity. Relative to the synthetic minority over-sampling technique (SMOTE), GenPFN provides lower coverage distance and greater diversity. Among observed paired regression fits, augmentation reduces estimated AutoGluon validation mean squared error by 62.1% relative to context-only training. A hull-stern case study yields 99.3% propeller-compatible candidates versus 1.4% among randomly sampled context designs. Generation followed by evaluation produces sample sets that augment limited datasets and support training more accurate predictive models.

title: TRACE: Target-Trial Relevance Assessment and Compatibility-Guided Evidence Synthesis
summary: External trial evidence can inform oncology trial design, but broad pooling may produce benchmarks poorly aligned with the planned population. We developed TRACE (Target-Trial Relevance Assessment and Compatibility-Guided Evidence Synthesis), combining eligibility screening, Bayesian compatibility assessment using published baseline characteristics, and hierarchical survival modeling. An integrated compatibility score based on the largest standardized difference in jointly reported characteristics identifies compatible external trials. Their reconstructed control-arm survival data are synthesized using a hierarchical beta-Stacy process to generate a predictive survival benchmark. We evaluated TRACE using eleven randomized phase III trials in first-line HER2-negative advanced gastric/gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma. With KEYNOTE-859 as the target, three external trials were selected. TRACE predicted a control-arm median overall survival of 11.8 months (95% posterior predictive interval, 8.9-15.2), compared with an observed median of 11.8 months (95% confidence interval, 10.9-12.7). In leave-one-trial-out validation, seven targets had compatible external evidence. Predictive intervals contained the observed median for all seven. In comparison, confidence intervals from Kaplan-Meier estimates pooling all other trials' control arms contained it for five. Mean pointwise curve coverage was 92% for TRACE and 59% for pooled Kaplan-Meier. For four targets without compatible external evidence, TRACE returned a weakly informative prior predictive benchmark. TRACE provides a transparent approach to selecting relevant external evidence and generating benchmarks for oncology trial planning.

title: Incremental Model Predictive Control for Reference Tracking of Nonlinear Anesthesia Dynamics
summary: Anesthesia dynamics are commonly described by Wiener models, consisting of linear dynamics followed by a static nonlinearity. This nonlinear output complicates the derivation of theoretical guarantees on closed-loop stability and convergence. Model Predictive Control (MPC) is particularly suitable for anesthesia control, as it explicitly accounts for constraints in the control design. In this paper, we propose an incremental MPC formulation for tracking a desired reference. The proposed approach exploits the structure of the nonlinear output equation to reformulate the control problem within a linear framework. An incremental model is then employed to avoid the explicit computation of steady states and inputs, which may be inaccurate in the presence of model uncertainties. The proposed controller is evaluated through simulations involving 1000 virtual patients and compared with a benchmark MPC formulation. Results show improved steady-state reference tracking while maintaining satisfactory disturbance rejection.

title: OverServe: Resource Amplification Attacks on SaaS Agents via Tool--Prompt Co-Design
summary: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are enabling software-as-a-service (SaaS) providers to automate longer business workflows with agents. In subscription-based SaaS deployments, model and tool calls consume provider resources without additional customer payments. Because the agent autonomously decides when to stop, a malicious tenant can send a prompt to the agent, exploiting its completion decisions to extend execution and waste provider resources. In this paper, we present OverServe, a multi-agent framework for constructing such attacks against SaaS agents. OverServe co-designs Model Context Protocol (MCP) status tools and completion-confirmation prompts for the attacker. Each tool call returns accurate status and terminates normally, yet the agent may repeatedly check an unfinished condition to satisfy the prompt. This consumes the SaaS provider's resources even after the original business task is completed. OverServe constructs service-specific tool--prompt pairs and uses separate tool and prompt reviews to guide candidate pair selection. Tested tool specifications trigger no alerts in the evaluated MCP scanners. We evaluate Qwen, Nemotron, DeepSeek, and Sonnet on selected tasks from nine benchmarks. All OverServe runs pass the original task checks. OverServe can reach a maximal amplification of API requests by $93.88\times$ while preserving the original task goal and collateral checks.

title: Stochastic Kernel Mode Decomposition: Information, Uncertainty, and Conditional Regime Inference
summary: When do mode energies preserve regime information as measurement quality changes? Stochastic Kernel Mode Decomposition (sKMD) fits joint regime laws on signed KMD mode coordinates and transfers the reference mode posterior to regime probabilities and conditional reconstructions. For centered Gaussian regimes with independently varying known noise variances, fixed coordinate energies retain the full regime posterior precisely when all classes share their cross-covariances and class variances can differ only at isolated vertices of the covariance graph. We extend the characterization to nonzero means and show that freely varying correlated noise forces a fixed linear log-odds decoder to retain the full quadratic feature span even for two distinct centered regimes. At fixed quality, a three-regime example has no sufficient two-energy basis. Its smallest Bayes log-loss gap over bases of condition number at most $κ$ has sharp order $κ^{-1}$. Exact Bayes energy posteriors supply numerical gap estimates for specified bases. Additional bounds relate feature compression, independently learned mode spans and sensor-noise error to log loss. Two controlled experiments with 64 independent panels each show that signed information can improve prediction over energy summaries, while integration gives small gains over strong signed controls and depends on how the competing point rule is calibrated and how accurately observation noise is measured.

title: Delta-Iterations: A General-Purpose Linear Regression Solver for Huber's Penalty, $ε$-Insensitive Loss, and Other Moreau Envelope-Based Loss Functions
comment: Submitted to Signal Processing (Elsevier), Matlab Code is available at Codeocean : https://doi.org/10.24433/CO.2122644.v1
summary: A general-purpose linear regression solver for a class of smooth loss functions is presented. The method applies to loss functions of the Moreau envelope type, which are continuously differentiable and have Lipschitz-continuous first derivatives. This class includes piecewise-defined cost functions consisting of constant, linear and quadratic segments, such as Huber's loss, insensitive least squares, one-sided least squares. The convergence guarantee provided by the associated proximal operator, the simplicity of the method and its versatility in handling various cost functions within a unified framework are its main advantages. MATLAB code for reproducing the numerical results presented in this article is provided.

title: BirdDreams: Joint Perspective and BEV Video Generation for a Plausible, Reactive Driving World Model
summary: Driving world models aim to simulate how a scene unfolds under different ego actions. This requires plausible motion of surrounding vehicles as well as precise ego-trajectory control. Learning vehicle motion from perspective video alone is challenging because motion is entangled with appearance and vehicles can be occluded. Prior work therefore conditions video generation on layouts that specify vehicle motion, providing control over surrounding vehicles but requiring their future trajectories as inputs. We introduce BirdDreams, an autoregressive driving world model that jointly generates perspective video and a schematic bird's-eye-view (BEV) video, making scene layout part of the predicted future. The BEV, rendered from scene annotations for training, depicts roads and vehicles as simple shapes at a fixed metric scale, providing a top-down view of their positions and motion with reduced occlusion between vehicles. Perspective video, by contrast, retains scene details that the BEV omits, such as traffic signals and object appearance. Joint attention between two video diffusion transformers, one per stream, lets each stream inform the other during generation. The predicted BEV also provides a geometric interface for ego control: we translate and rotate its latest frame along an input ego trajectory and use the resulting frames as a soft condition that shows how the scene would appear to move if only the ego vehicle moved. At inference, BirdDreams generates both videos from a single camera image without requiring an HD map or vehicle-state inputs. On PhysicalAI-AV and nuScenes, BirdDreams follows input ego trajectories more faithfully than prior driving world models and generates more plausible ego motion without ego-action conditioning. Human evaluation shows that BirdDreams outperforms a perspective-only baseline in generating realistic surrounding-vehicle behavior.

title: Identifiability and partial identification under spatial confounding in additive risk models
summary: In spatial risk attribution, continuous environmental exposures and unmeasured background factors often co-vary across broad geographic scales, making it difficult to separate true exposure effects from spatial confounding using finite disease counts. Existing remedies typically project out or penalize shared spatial trends, leaving unclear whether estimation instability stems from the overall capacity of the latent random field or from its directional alignment with exposure. By decomposing the Fisher-weighted smoothing operator of an additive Poisson point process model, we show that while effective degrees of freedom measure total smoothing capacity, the relative loss of Fisher information for the exposure coefficient is governed solely by a distinct directional quantity that we call penalized collinear overlap. Rotating the spatial kernel alters this information loss while holding total capacity fixed, implying that no single smoothing scale is universally optimal. Because real-world confounding combines smooth regional trends with sharp local jumps that escape any moderate basis dictionary, point identification remains fragile. We therefore develop a partial identification framework that bounds residual confounding bias using an observable benchmark covariate. Projecting a joint spatial confidence ellipse yields valid intervals even under weak benchmarks, while incorporating a negative control outcome sharpens the bounds and flags assumption violations. Simulation studies and an analysis of childhood respiratory mortality across England demonstrate the method.

title: Can STATCOM and UPS-Based Voltage Support Mitigate Fault-Induced Reductions in AI Data Center Grid Power Draw?
summary: Artificial intelligence data centers (AIDCs) are rapidly increasing in number and capacity. These large electronic loads are interfaced through power electronic devices and can sharply reduce grid power intake during fault-induced voltage sags. Disturbances exceeding equipment ride-through capabilities may also trigger protective disconnection, posing risks to power system security. Static synchronous compensators (STATCOMs) and appropriately controlled AIDC uninterruptible power supply (UPS) rectifiers can provide reactive power support during voltage sags. This paper compares the individual and combined effectiveness of STATCOM and UPS-based voltage support in mitigating fault-induced reductions in grid power intake through electromagnetic transient simulations of a 1 GW AIDC connected to an IEEE nine-bus system. Simulation results show that STATCOM support better preserves short-term intake in milder tested faults, whereas UPS coordination maintains rectifier operation under deeper sags by reducing active intake to reserve reactive current capacity. Combined support improves auxiliary load retention and recovery in selected cases. However, severe tested sags still cause substantial grid-demand reductions even with combined support.

title: Tripod Reordering: A 33-Queue Layout of Planar Graphs
summary:
A queue layout of a graph consists of a linear order of the vertices and a partition of the edges into queues so that no two edges in a single queue are nested. The minimum number of queues needed in a queue layout of a graph is called its queue number. A planar product structure theorem of Dujmović, Joret, Micek, Morin, Ueckerdt, and Wood (JACM, 2020) states that every planar graph is a subgraph of the strong product of a graph of simple treewidth at most $3$, a clique $K_3$, and a path. The result has been used to show that the queue number of planar graphs is at most $49$.
  Recently, Bekos, Gronemann, and Raftopoulou (Algorithmica, 2023) investigated how the general approach based on the product structure can be optimized for planar graphs. They claim that an appropriate reordering of the three vertices associated with each bag in the product structure decomposition, called a tripod, reduces the queue number of planar graphs to $42$. We first highlight a gap in their queue layout algorithm: one of the choices required by the algorithm is not guaranteed to exist. Then we show how to address the limitation and provide an alternative tripod reordering mechanism that reduces the upper bound on the queue number of planar graphs to $33$. As a corollary, bipartite planar graphs have queue number at most $22$.

title: Sticky Manifold Piecewise Deterministic Monte Carlo for Bayesian Model Averaging
summary: Assigning positive prior probability to lower-dimensional submodels enriches the range of uncertainty that Bayesian models can represent. The resulting posterior distributions combine continuous parameter uncertainty with discrete model uncertainty. Efficient movement between these submodels, however, can be difficult to design. We propose the sticky manifold construction as a principled, modular framework for combining piecewise deterministic Markov processes (PDMPs) across different submodels. The integration is rejection-free, requires no additional likelihood evaluations, and retains the non-reversible and ballistic nature of the component PDMP dynamics. We prove that the resulting process leaves the intended mixed-dimensional target invariant. We also develop a manifold PDMP algorithm based on coordinate charts to provide the within-submodel dynamics and a blow-up procedure that resolves singular sets into codimension-one sticky boundaries. This geometric construction makes the remaining design choices explicit; component dynamics and unsticking kernels can be chosen freely, subject to easily verifiable velocity compatibility conditions. Finally, we demonstrate the sticky manifold algorithms in Bayesian model averaging examples, propagating uncertainty over pure versus mixed states in quantum state tomography, rank in Bayesian principal component analysis, and parametric families in survival extrapolation.

title: Certified Dynamic Subspace Optimization for Bayesian ISAC Design
comment: 19 pages, 10 figures, submitted to IEEE journal
summary: Full-space covariance optimization is costly in large-array Bayesian integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). A fixed transmit subspace can reduce this cost, but the resulting optimality loss depends on the posterior distribution. In this paper, a certified dynamic subspace method is developed for angle Bayesian Cramér-Rao bound (BCRB) minimization under joint angle and complex-gain uncertainty. For uniform linear arrays, exact response preservation over a nondegenerate posterior angular interval requires the full antenna space. Subspace sufficiency is therefore assessed through full-space objective-gap bounds. A communication-feasible basis is initialized from the user-channel span and local BCRB sensitivity. Restricted semidefinite programs are then solved. Primal restoration and dual repair yield gap bounds that remain valid after lossless user-beam recovery. When an accurate restricted solve does not certify the requested tolerance, the basis is expanded using a direction identified from the covariance dual slacks.
